newsitem.title: INDIA: Rao exit throws India party into leadership crisis.
newsitem.headline: Rao exit throws India party into leadership crisis.

text.p: The resignation of former Prime Minister P.V. Narasimha Rao from his last post in India's Congress party has caused a leadership crisis in the country's oldest political machine, analysts said on Thursday.

Rao, who was prime minister from 1991 until earlier this year, resigned as leader of the party's parliamentary delegation on Thursday following a party resolution and a directive from Congress president Sitaram Kesri asking him to step down.
"Congress is facing a crisis of leadership. There is no natural leader. Nobody has a track record one can trust," political columnist Kewal Varma told Reuters.
The order from Kesri was the last assault in a gradually mounting leadership challenge after Rao led the party to its worst electoral defeat in general elections in May this year.
In September, Rao resigned as party president after a court upheld a summons asking him to testify as a co-accused in a case of criminal conspiracy. Rao denied any wrongdoing in the case.

Rao continued to wield clout as head of the parliamentary delegation that offers crucial support to Prime Minister Deve Gowda's centre-left coalition. The Congress has 142 deputies in the 545-member federal parliament.

The 75-year-old leader headed the party for five years and held it together despite lacking the charisma of the Nehru-Gandhi political family, whose members have led the party for most of the years since independence from Britian in 1947.
Rao introduced free-market reforms to change the face of the staunchly socialist Congress party, which has ruled India for all but five years since 1947.

But a number of corruption cases that embroiled Rao and his senior aides were widely seen as having damaged the party's image. Rao has denied any wrongdoing in the cases which involve accusations of cheating, forgery and bribery.
Yubaraj Ghimire, assistant editor of "Outlook" magazine, said Rao's power base in the party had been eroded by the delay in his resignation.
"Had there been some grace, had he resigned a few days ago, he would have had some role in leadership," Ghimire said.

Varma said leaders like Sharad Pawar, widely seen as the prime contender along with Kesri himself in a race to succeed Rao as head of the parliamentary delegation, lacked the necessary appeal to consolidate the Congress.

"Pawar has been on a downtrend for the past four years. Others have not proved anything. Many of them are handsome faces, that's all," Varma said, adding that Kesri, older than Rao, could not draw mass support to help the party.
But Rao's exit is seen as a boon to clean up the Congress.

"A large number of Congressmen...are silently hoping that with his departure, the taint of corruption that has dogged the party in recent times will also go," the Asian Age newspaper said on Thursday.
The Congress still enjoyed countrywide popularity and remained the prime party potentially stronger than other groups appealing to Hindu caste or religious sentiments, Varma said.
"The situation is favourable for Congress. Other parties have been sectarian. You cannot run a heterogeneous country with a sectarian support base," Varma said.

He said Deve Gowda, who formed a 13-party United Front coalition with support from the Congress this year, could face trouble if the Congress threw up a new parliamentary leader impatient to win power himself.
"Deve Gowda's future depends on who succeeds Rao. There could be a problem between Congress and United Front," Varma said.
